passage: In the study hall of the boarding school, Rashmi's phone lay face up beside her chemistry notes. Jatin's message had been sitting there since 7:40: "u ok? u left dinner early." She had read it eleven times. She wasn't going to answer. If she said what was wrong, that he'd laughed along when the others mocked her accent at dinner, he would probably say, "Relax, you're overreacting." Silence felt safer. Silence felt like the one thing she could control. Ramesh sir walked between the desks, checking that phones were away. Rashmi slid hers under her notebook but kept one corner visible, just in case it lit up again. Part of her wanted Jatin to keep trying. To notice. To come and find her.

qa.q: Since what time had Jatin's message been sitting there?
qa.a: It had been sitting there since 7:40.

qa.q: Why does Rashmi choose not to reply?
qa.a: She fears hearing "you're overreacting", so silence feels safer and gives her some control.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Rashmi now?
qa.a: She could reply briefly with the real reason, "The accent jokes at dinner hurt", rather than waiting for Jatin to guess.

qa.q: What is Jatin likely experiencing as his message goes unanswered?
qa.a: Jatin is probably unsure and uneasy, noticing something is wrong but not knowing what he did.

grounding: Shows a teen girl withholding a reply because silence feels safer than a fight, while hoping her friend will notice and come to her.

passage:
Dear Uday,
I'm not going to send this. That's kind of the point. You've texted me four times since Saturday's practice, and I've left every one on "seen". I know it's mean. But if I reply, I'll have to say that it hurt when you told Coach I wasn't ready for the relay, like I'm the weakest girl on the team, and you'll say I'm too sensitive, and then we'll fight, and I'll cry, and you'll win. Not replying means I don't lose. It's the only part of this I'm in charge of. And honestly? Some small, silly part of me hopes you'll keep texting. That you'll show up at my gate and say, "Pallavi, what's wrong?" Then I'd know you actually care.
Your friend (for now)

qa.q: How many times has Uday texted since Saturday's practice?
qa.a: Uday has texted four times since Saturday's practice.

qa.q: What does Pallavi secretly hope will happen?
qa.a: She hopes Uday will keep texting and even come to her gate asking what's wrong, which would prove Uday cares.

qa.q: What could Pallavi try instead of leaving every message on "seen"?
qa.a: She could send one honest line, "What you told Coach hurt me", and ask Uday to hear it without calling her sensitive.

qa.q: What might Uday be feeling after four unanswered texts?
qa.a: Uday may feel worried and shut out, unable to guess what went wrong, and might soon stop trying.

grounding: Shows a teen girl choosing silence as protection from a fight and from being called too sensitive, while hoping her friend will come to her.

passage:
"Vinita, wait up!" Vandana caught her at the school gate. "You didn't reply yesterday. Or this morning."
"Battery died."
"You were online. I saw."
Vinita shrugged and kept walking.
"Are you angry with me?"
"No."
"Is it about Saturday?"
"I said no."
Vandana stopped. "Okay. Fine."
Vinita kept her eyes on the road. If she said it, Vandana would laugh and say she was overreacting, like last time. Silence was safer. At least silence was hers.
But three steps later, she slowed down, just a little, in case Vandana would follow and ask one more time.

qa.q: What excuse did Vinita give for not replying?
qa.a: She said her battery died.

qa.q: Why did Vinita choose to stay silent?
qa.a: She was afraid Vandana would laugh and call her overreacting, so silence felt safer and gave her a sense of control, while part of her hoped Vandana would keep asking.

qa.q: What turning point is available at this stage?
qa.a: Vinita could say one honest sentence, such as "Saturday hurt me," and give Vandana a chance to answer, instead of hoping to be chased.

qa.q: What is Vandana experiencing when she says "Okay. Fine"?
qa.a: She feels frustrated and shut out, not knowing what she did, and gives up asking.

grounding: A teenage girl withholds replies because silence feels safer than risking a fight, while quietly hoping her friend will notice and come after her.

passage:
I remember the week I didn't answer Jatin.
He'd made that joke about my drawing in front of the art class. Everyone laughed, and I laughed too. But I went home with my face burning.
When he texted that night, "u ok?", I didn't reply. Not the next day either. If I told him it hurt, he'd say what my brother always says: "You're overreacting, it was a joke." I couldn't take hearing that again.
Not replying made me feel strong, like I was holding all the cards.
But honestly? Every time my phone lit up, I hoped it was him. I wanted him to notice. I wanted him to come find me. I'm Vidya, I was a girl of fourteen, and silence felt like my only armour.

qa.q: What did Jatin text Vidya that night?
qa.a: "u ok?"

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling while not replying to Jatin?
qa.a: Vidya felt hurt and afraid of being told she was overreacting, but also strangely strong and in control, while secretly hoping he would come find her.

qa.q: What turning point was available to Vidya that week?
qa.a: Vidya could have replied to Jatin's "u ok?" with the truth, that the joke hurt, rather than using silence as armour.

qa.q: What might Jatin have been experiencing during that week?
qa.a: He likely felt confused and worried, since he reached out and got no answer.

grounding: A teen recalls withholding replies after a hurtful joke because silence felt safer and gave control, while secretly hoping the friend would come.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 10A, Friday

Mehak has been unusually quiet all week. On Monday I saw Imran try to hand her the chemistry notes; she took them without looking at him. On Wednesday he asked her something at the water cooler. She answered with one word.
When I asked her after class if anything was wrong, she said, "It's easier not to talk. If I say what happened, it'll just become a big fight." She said it firmly, but twice during our talk she glanced at the door, as if expecting someone.
I told her that silence can protect you for a while but can also leave you lonely. I offered to sit with both of them on Monday if she wants.

qa.q: What did Mehak take from Imran on Monday?
qa.a: The chemistry notes.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling when she said it was easier not to talk?
qa.a: She felt guarded and afraid of a big fight, and her glances at the door suggest she also hoped someone, perhaps Imran, would come.

qa.q: What turning point did the teacher offer?
qa.a: The teacher gently named the cost of silence and offered to sit with both of them on Monday, making speaking feel safer.

qa.q: What is Imran experiencing this week?
qa.a: He seems to be trying to reach Mehak with notes and questions, and is likely confused and hurt by her one-word answers.

grounding: A teacher notices a teenage girl withholding words from a friend because silence feels safer than a fight, while she seems to hope he will come to her.

passage:
Thursday night

Siddharth has messaged four times since Tuesday. "Hey?" "U ok?" "Did I do something?" and a meme.

I haven't replied to any of them. I read them on the lock screen so the blue ticks don't show.

Why? Because if I tell him I'm hurt that he told everyone about my audition, he'll say, "Binita, you're overreacting, it was good news!" And then I'll cry in front of him, which is worse.

This way I'm in control. I decide when we talk. Nobody can call me dramatic if I don't say anything.

But the weird part: every time my phone buzzes, I hope it's him. I kind of want him to keep trying. To realise on his own.

Is that fair? Probably not. I'm still not replying tonight.

qa.q: How many times has Siddharth messaged since Tuesday?
qa.a: Siddharth has messaged four times since Tuesday.

qa.q: What does Binita hope for while staying silent?
qa.a: Binita feels hurt and wary but secretly hopes Siddharth will keep trying and understand without being told.

qa.q: What could Binita try instead of staying silent?
qa.a: Binita could reply briefly, 'I was hurt you told everyone about the audition, can we talk?', which is honest without starting a fight.

qa.q: How might Siddharth be feeling after four unanswered messages?
qa.a: Siddharth is likely confused and worried, unsure what he did and anxious that the friendship is slipping.

grounding: A teen withholds replies to feel safe and in control, fearing being called overreacting, while hoping the friend will notice and reach out first.
